subject: physics

items.q: How can radio waves be produced?
items.correct: By oscillations in an electrical circuit
items.misconception: By changes in the nucleus of an atom
items.why: Once students learn that changes in atoms and nuclei generate electromagnetic waves over a wide frequency range, they generalise it to the whole spectrum and forget that the specification gives radio waves an electrical source. For radio waves the specification gives a circuit source: they can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. Only gamma rays are attributed to changes in the nucleus of an atom.
items.random_wrong: By changes in the electrons of an atom

items.q: Which statement best describes what happens when a radio wave is absorbed by an electrical circuit?
items.correct: It induces oscillations, creating an alternating current
items.misconception: It creates a direct current in one fixed direction
items.why: Students think of absorption as the wave delivering a single push of energy, and their default picture of current from any supply is the steady, one-direction current of a cell. The wave oscillates, so the current it creates oscillates with it. When radio waves are absorbed they may create an alternating current — the wave induces oscillations in the circuit.
items.random_wrong: It heats the circuit but produces no current at all

items.q: A transmitter circuit oscillates at 200 kHz and emits a radio wave. A distant circuit absorbs that wave. What alternating current is induced in the distant circuit?
items.correct: 200 kHz, the same as the radio wave
items.misconception: 400 kHz, twice that of the radio wave
items.why: Students who have seen a full wave cycle drawn as 'two pushes' count the pushes rather than the cycles, and others assume the receiving circuit imposes its own rate on whatever arrives. The specification is precise: the alternating current created has the same frequency as the radio wave itself. A 95 MHz wave induces a 95 MHz alternating current.
items.random_wrong: 0 Hz, since a direct current is induced

items.correct: In changes in the nucleus of an atom
items.misconception: In oscillations in an electrical circuit
items.why: Once students learn that changes in atoms and nuclei generate electromagnetic waves over a wide frequency range, they generalise it to the whole spectrum and forget that the specification gives radio waves an electrical source. For radio waves the specification gives a circuit source: they can be produced by oscillations in electrical circuits. Only gamma rays are attributed to changes in the nucleus of an atom.
items.random_wrong: In the vibration of the whole atom

items.q: A student writes: 'X-rays must come from the nucleus, because they are ionising like gamma rays.' What is wrong with this?
items.correct: Only gamma rays are stated to come from the nucleus
items.misconception: Nothing is wrong; all ionising radiation is nuclear
items.why: X-rays and gamma rays are named together as ionising radiation with similar hazards, so students assume they must also share an origin. 'Nuclear' and 'dangerous' become the same idea in their minds. Sharing a hazard is not sharing an origin. The specification names X-rays and gamma rays together as ionising radiation, but only gamma rays are said to originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.
items.random_wrong: Gamma rays come from the electrons, not the nucleus

items.q: What does a radiation dose, given in sieverts, measure?
items.correct: The risk of harm from an exposure to radiation
items.misconception: The number of gamma rays that reach the body
items.why: 'Dose' sounds like a quantity of a substance, as with a dose of medicine, so students read it as an amount rather than as a measure of risk. Radiation dose measures the risk of harm from an exposure. It reflects both the size of the exposure and the type of radiation, because the effects depend on both.
items.random_wrong: The frequency of the radiation absorbed

items.q: Two people are exposed to the same type of radiation, but one receives four times the dose of the other. What conclusion can be drawn?
items.correct: The greater dose carries the greater risk of harm
items.misconception: The risk is the same, as the type of radiation is the same
items.why: The types are taught as a ranked list of hazards, which invites students to treat 'gamma' as a fixed level of danger and to drop the amount of exposure from the argument entirely. Both matter. The specification says the effects depend on the type of radiation and the size of the dose, which is why dose is measured and recorded at all.
items.random_wrong: The risk depends only on how long each exposure was

items.q: A worker receives a radiation dose of 2500 mSv. What is this dose in sieverts (Sv)?
items.why: Prefixes are treated as decoration attached to the unit rather than as a factor, so students rewrite the unit and leave the value untouched. The prefix is a factor of 1000. Every conversion between mSv and Sv changes the number by 1000, so 2500 mSv becomes 2.5 Sv.

items.q: A table gives these average doses: chest X-ray 0.02 mSv; CT scan of the abdomen 8 mSv; natural background radiation 2.7 mSv per year. Which conclusion is valid?
items.correct: One CT scan gives about three years' worth of background
items.misconception: A CT scan is certain to cause that patient to get cancer
items.why: Media reporting and the phrase 'radiation causes cancer' present the link as certain, and students have little experience of writing conclusions in terms of risk. Radiation dose is a measure of the risk of harm resulting from an exposure. Conclusions drawn from dose data should be written as increased or decreased risk, never as a guaranteed consequence.
items.random_wrong: One chest X-ray gives a larger dose than one CT scan

items.q: Worker A receives a dose of 800 mSv in a year. Worker B receives 1.2 Sv in the same year. Who receives the larger dose?
items.correct: B, because 1.2 Sv is 1200 mSv, more than A's 800 mSv
items.misconception: A, because 800 is a much bigger number than 1.2 is
items.why: Under time pressure students compare the numbers in front of them and treat the unit as a label rather than as part of the value, especially when one number is small and looks unimportant. Convert to a common unit before comparing. Using 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, 1.2 Sv is 1200 mSv, so it is the larger dose and carries the greater risk of harm.
items.random_wrong: Neither, because the two doses are equal once converted

items.q: Which hazardous effect on the human body is caused by ultraviolet waves?
items.correct: Premature ageing of the skin and skin cancer risk
items.misconception: Heating of the whole body from the inside outwards
items.why: Heating is the effect students have already met for infrared and microwaves, so it becomes their general explanation for how any electromagnetic wave harms the body. The hazard named for X-rays and gamma rays is ionisation: they are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
items.random_wrong: Immediate burning of tissue deep inside the body

items.q: Why are X-rays and gamma rays described as hazardous to human body tissue?
items.correct: They are ionising and can cause gene mutation and cancer
items.misconception: They heat body tissue very quickly, causing severe burns
items.why: Heating is the effect students have already met for infrared and microwaves, so it becomes their general explanation for how any electromagnetic wave harms the body. The hazard named for X-rays and gamma rays is ionisation: they are ionising radiation that can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
items.random_wrong: They age the skin, but do not reach the deeper tissue

items.q: Where do gamma rays come from?
items.correct: Gamma rays originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.
items.misconception: Gamma rays are given out by the electrons of an atom, in the same way that light is.
items.why: Students meet electrons moving and giving out radiation before they meet gamma rays, so they apply the picture they already have to every high-energy wave. Diagrams of atoms also draw attention to the electrons rather than the nucleus. The specification distinguishes the two: changes in atoms and the nuclei of atoms can both produce electromagnetic waves over a wide frequency range, but gamma rays specifically originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do you convert 2500 mSv into sieverts?
items.correct: Divide by 1000, because 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv). 2500 mSv = 2.5 Sv.
items.misconception: The sievert is the bigger unit, so you multiply by 1000 to change millisieverts into sieverts.
items.why: Students remember that the two units differ by a factor of 1000 but not which way round, and 'bigger unit, so multiply' feels right without checking that it makes the answer absurdly large. Check the size of the answer. Since 1000 mSv = 1 Sv, a dose in mSv always gives a smaller number in Sv, so you divide by 1000.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.correct: The specification names X-rays and gamma rays as ionising radiation.
items.misconception: Ultraviolet must be ionising too, because it causes cancer.
items.why: Students link the word 'cancer' to the word 'ionising' and treat them as the same statement, so any radiation described as causing cancer gets labelled ionising. Ultraviolet waves are hazardous — they can cause skin to age prematurely and increase the risk of skin cancer — but it is X-rays and gamma rays that the specification identifies as ionising radiation causing the mutation of genes and cancer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.correct: A background dose is a real exposure and carries a risk of harm, and is often the yardstick other doses are compared with.
items.misconception: Background radiation is natural, so it is harmless and can be left out when you compare doses.
items.why: Students equate 'natural' with 'safe', and background radiation is described as something everyone receives all the time, which makes it sound like nothing is happening. Dose measures risk of harm whatever the source. When drawing conclusions from data, background dose is included and is frequently the useful comparison — for example, expressing a scan as so many years' worth of background.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays affect the body in the same way?
items.correct: No. Ultraviolet ages skin prematurely and increases skin cancer risk; X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and can cause the mutation of genes and cancer.
items.misconception: They are all hazardous, so they all do the same thing to the body.
items.why: The three are listed together in one sentence about hazardous effects on human body tissue, so students store one hazard for the group instead of the specific effects the specification gives. Keep the effects separate. The specification states that the effects depend on the type of radiation, and gives the skin effects for ultraviolet and the ionising, gene-mutation effects for X-rays and gamma rays.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.6.2.3 Properties of electromagnetic waves 2
